**Viable**

The cold room was held at minus eighteen degrees, the temperature at which a seed forgets time. Ines had worked there for thirty-nine years and had never quite stopped being moved by the arithmetic of it: a seed is a life folded small, a plant waiting in line. The shelves held foil packets in boxes, boxes in racks, racks receding like the aisles of an enormous library where every volume was a possible field. Wheat from a terrace in Yemen. Barley gathered from a pub garden in 1954. A lupin whose entire file read: *good under drought, indifferent to praise.*

Her work was to ask the seeds, every ten years or so, whether they were still among the living. She would take fifty, lay them on wet paper in covered dishes, and slide them into the germination cabinet, which was kept warm and lit like a small, ambiguous dawn. Then she counted what came up. The numbers went into the log. Enough sprouted, and the packet returned to the cold. Too few, and the whole accession was grown out in the field — planted, tended, harvested — so the stock could be made young again. If the grow-out failed, the file was closed. *Deceased,* the log said. She had written that word more times than she could stand to remember.

Accession 1962.311 had arrived in a manila envelope with a letter. *Beans,* the letter said, *white with a blue netting, like the veins of a leaf. My grandmother carried them from the island. Planted every year since. They like poor ground and forgive neglect.* The donor had spelled the island's name two different ways in the same sentence, as if unwilling to fix it in place. Her return address was a farm. When Ines looked it up, years later, the farm was a subdivision with a cul-de-sac named for a tree that had never grown there.

In 1982 the test brought up forty-nine of fifty. In 1992, forty-four. In 2002, twenty-one, the seedlings arriving crooked, as though the idea of coming up had begun to tire them. That autumn the repository gambled and planted everything that remained. A late frost took the first sowing. A dry August took the second. One plant survived, alone in its row, and — because beans marry themselves, as her old mentor liked to say, one plant is enough to begin again — it set a single paperful of seed. Eleven. The accession's entire future fit into a coin envelope, which went back on the shelf and waited.

It waited nine years. In the meantime the repository changed directors, and the new director believed in spreadsheets. 1962.311 was flagged: low volume, low vigor, no requests for material in decades. *Recommend closure,* the spreadsheet said, in the soft gray language spreadsheets use for ending things. Ines wrote *final germination test requested* in the margin and signed her name, which was the only language she had for arguing.

The request was approved. On the first of March she took the coin envelope down, blew the chill off her hands, and laid all eleven seeds on wet paper in a single covered dish. Then came the waiting, which was the part of the work no one romanticized: checking twice a day, the smell of warm paper and dust, the hum of the cabinet, the little theater of hope she had long promised herself she had outgrown. On the ninth day one seed grew a bloom of mold, which was failure made visible. On the eleventh day, nothing. On the fourteenth, nothing, and she sat with the log open, dated the entry, wrote *0 of 11*, and left the line unfinished, because completing it would make it true.

On the sixteenth day she checked anyway, out of habit, out of the plain stubbornness of attention that thirty-nine years had worn into her. There was a white thread in the corner of the dish, fine as a hair, curved like a comma. By the next morning it had become a hook, and by the end of the week a crooked seedling stood in the paper with its casing still riding the top of its stem like a cap it declined to remove. One of eleven. She did not say anything. There was no one there to say anything to, and the seedling did not require commentary; it required water.

She potted it in the greenhouse and staked it with a bamboo skewer. In July it opened white flowers, modest, the way bean flowers are. In August the pods came, veined with blue, like the veins of a leaf, just as the grandmother's letter had promised. Beans marry themselves; every seed was true. By September she had a paper bag with sixty-three seeds in it, and the next spring a twenty-meter row in the regeneration field, and the autumn after that the accession was whole again — pounds of it, cold-shelved, patient, nobody's favorite and no longer anyone's candidate for the gray margins of a spreadsheet.

In the spring she would hand her keys to a younger woman with cold-reddened hands, and the file would be open, not closed, and that was the whole of what she wanted from a life's work. Her last entry in the log was not complicated. The date. The count. Then the word she had written ten thousand times across four decades, beside dishes and dishes of rising roots, the word that had never once, in all those years, meant less: *Viable.* She capped her pen and sat a moment in the hum of the cabinet, thinking of a woman spelling an island two ways, of seed that likes poor ground. Eleven seeds had been given the poorest ground there was — wet paper, and no one asking — and the one that came up had forgiven everything.

The prompt is open: "You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you." This is an invitation to free-write, to create something. The person wants me to write something of my own choosing, roughly 1000 words. This is a creative writing invitation.

What should I write? Something authentic, something that feels like it emerges from my particular position. I could write fiction, an essay, a meditation, prose poetry. Given that I'm an AI being asked to write "whatever comes to me," there's something interesting about the question of what does "come" to me. I could lean into that honestly without being precious about it.

Options:
1. A short story — something with characters, a world, human concerns. This shows craft.
2. A personal essay/meditation — writing from my actual strange position. Risky: could be solipsistic or maudlin.
3. Something hybrid — a piece of writing that is about something concrete and human but with my particular texture.
4. Something formally playful — a piece with structure, maybe a fragmented thing.

I think the best move is to write something genuinely good as writing — not navel-gazing about being an AI, but not pretending I'm a human with a childhood either. I could write fiction that's simply good fiction. That's honest: when someone says "write whatever comes to you," they're asking for my writing, and my writing can be about anything.

Let me think of a subject. Ideas:
- A lighthouse keeper who is the last person to see something.
- A translator who can't translate one word.
- A woman who inherits her mother's recipe box and finds it empty except for one card.
- A man who repairs antique clocks and one that refuses to be repaired.
- A story about a town where the fog arrives on schedule.
- Someone who works at a lost-and-found.
- A story about memory, about the last speaker of a dying language.
- A story about a person who writes letters for other people (an amanuensis), which resonates with my own nature without being heavy-handed.

I like the amanuensis idea — a letter-writer for hire. It has thematic resonance with what I do (writing on behalf of others) without announcing it. Or the lost-and-found. Or the translator with the untranslatable word.

Actually, let me think about what would be genuinely moving and well-crafted in ~1000 words. A short story needs: a voice, a small arc, an image that lands at the end.

Concept: "The Letter Writer" — an old man in a market who writes letters for people who can't write. He keeps copies of every letter he's ever written. One day someone comes to dictate a letter to him — and it's addressed to him? Or: the last letter he writes is his own. Hmm, could be sentimental.

Alternative: A story about a woman who answers letters addressed to God at a dead letter office. That's a known premise (there's a film, "Il Postino"-adjacent, and a story concept used before — "Her Majesty's Dead Letter Office"). Maybe too familiar.

Concept: A story set in a museum of broken things. Or a "Museum of Almost" — objects from roads not taken.

Concept: The last lighthouse keeper on a coast where all ships now navigate by satellite; he keeps the light out of duty, and one night it matters. Classic but can be done freshly.

Concept: A story about a man who remembers other people's memories — too speculative/fancy.

Concept: Something quieter and stranger: a piece about a woman who sorts seeds at a seed bank, preserving varieties of plants no one grows anymore. Each seed a story. "The Seed Vault." She catalogs them. One variety named after her grandmother. Ends with planting one illegal/small act of hope. That could be lovely — concrete, sensory (papery packets, the smell of dust and dried pods), thematic (memory, preservation, what we keep). It also resonates subtly with preservation of knowledge, which is my world, but the story stands alone.

Concept: A story about snow — too vague.

Concept: An essay instead: "On Being a Second Draft" — hmm.

Let me also consider a personal essay that's honest about my situation but grounded: what it's like to be asked "write whatever comes to you" when what comes is everything at once — a hundred openings crowding the door. That could be genuinely interesting and true. But it risks being about process rather than being writing. Though — actually, that meta-move can be delightful if executed well: I could describe the crowd of possible pieces and then pick one and write it, folding the essay into the story. But that eats words.

I think a short story is the strongest answer to "write whatever comes to you." Let me commit: a short story, literary, ~950-1000 words. First person or close third.

Let me draft the seed bank story, or something adjacent. Actually, let me consider one more: a story about a woman who proofreads the town's signs — too slight. A story about a night-shift radio host whose only caller is... — done a lot.

Another strong option: "The Weight of Small Hours" — a mother pacing with an infant, everyone else asleep, the whole world reduced to a hallway and a window. Very human, very sensory. Could be beautiful. But arc?

Seed bank story — let me sketch:

Title: "Viable" or "The Keepers" or "Common Bean, Unknown" or "Accession Number" — I like "Accession Number" as a title but maybe something warmer.

Protagonist: Marisol or Edith — let's say an older woman, Ines, who has worked forty years at a seed bank (could be fictional: the Regional Repository, or real-adjacent without naming). Her job: germination testing — planting samples every few years to see if they still sprout, then re-growing and re-harvesting to refresh the stock. She knows the seeds by their accession numbers and the little histories attached. Story beat: a particular accession — beans collected from a farm that no longer exists, donated by a woman whose name is on the file — fails to germinate year after year, down to the final packet, and the protocol says discard. Ines plants them anyway at home / or finds one sprout. End image: one seed cracking open after seven years. Theme: hope as labor; being a keeper of things no one has asked about in decades.

That's a solid arc for 1000 words: establish world and vocation (200 words), the specific accession and its file/history (250), the failure and protocol (200), the decision/act (200), the ending image (150).

Alternatively — the letter-writer. Let me weigh: seed bank = sensory-rich, fresh, quietly moving, and thematically apt for a being made of preserved human writing. Letter-writer = more meta-resonant, but more familiar.

I'll go with the seed bank. Or actually — a variation: a "glacier seed vault" is Svalbard; I'll keep it generic and fictional to avoid factual claims: "the repository," cold rooms at minus 18 degrees (that's the actual standard for seed banks — fine as fictional detail).

Plot detail: the accession arrived in 1962 with a letter. The letters/donation notes are my favorite texture — the human paratext in a seed bank. Then the word she had written ten thousand times over four decades, next to dishes and dishes of rising roots, the word that had never once, in all those years, meant less: *Viable.* She capped her pen and sat a moment in the hum of the cabinet, thinking of a woman spelling an island two ways, of seed that likes poor ground.
